In this last chapter "testimony" and "testify" come ten times (verses 6-11). The witnesses "testify" in 1:2; here God "has testified concerning his Son" (verse 9). The letter ends without a farewell, as it began without a greeting, but verse 20 returns to its opening words: "his Son, Jesus Christ" (1:3) and "eternal life" (1:2).

Earlier the letter names who "has been born" by what is done: righteousness (2:29), love (4:7). Verse 1 names them by what they believe, and joins believing to love, the two parts of the one commandment in 3:23. In 4:20 loving God was tested by loving the brother; verse 2 runs the test the other way. The believer of verse 1 holds what the liar of 2:22 denies, "that Jesus is the Christ," and verse 5 asks in the form of 2:22. The young men "have conquered" the evil one (2:13-14), the little children "them" (4:4); here, the world. Deuteronomy 30:11-14. The commandment is not too hard and not far away, but near, "to do it." Verse 3: his commandments "are not burdensome." John 14:15. Loving him goes with keeping his commandments; in verses 2-3, loving God does.

The letter has named blood once before, "the blood of Jesus his Son" (1:7), and water never. Verse 6 holds to both, "not in the water only," but does not say what they point to. In Greek "the one that testifies" (verse 6) is neuter, like "spirit"; "three who testify" (verse 7) is masculine, though spirit, water and blood are neuter nouns. Read "at one," the three agree; read "are one," they are united. Verse 11 says what God's testimony is: that he "gave us eternal life." Not believing God "has made him a liar," as saying "we have not sinned" does in 1:10. Deuteronomy 19:15. No matter stands on one witness. Verses 7-8 name three who testify, and they are "at one." John 19:34-35. Blood and water come from Jesus' side, and one who saw "has testified," the Greek verb and tense of verses 9-10. Verse 6 does not say whether it has this in view.

Verse 13 is the letter's last word about its own writing. In 4:6 the one who knows God "hears us"; in verse 14 the one we ask "hears us," the same two Greek words. "Ask" and "requests" share one Greek root; for sin toward death the verb changes to "make a request." The verse does not name who "will give him life," and the letter does not say what sin toward death is. John 20:30-31. The signs are written so that readers "may believe" and have life; verse 13, so that believers "may know" they have it. "The Christ, the Son of God" joins what is believed in verses 1 and 5. 1 Samuel 12:19. People who have sinned ask for prayer "so that we do not die," and Samuel calls it a sin to stop praying for them (1 Samuel 12:23). Verse 16 joins asking, sin and life.

Verse 18 has the words of 3:9, "everyone who has been born from God," with "does not sin" from 3:6. Two verses earlier a brother is seen "sinning" (verse 16). The letter has said, "If we say that we have no sin, we lead ourselves astray" (1:8), and "if anyone sins, we have an advocate" (2:1). Elsewhere the letter says "has been born"; here, once, "the one who was born," and the verse does not name him. Read "keeps him," there are two, the keeper and the kept; read "keeps himself," one. Read "in the evil one" (as in verse 18), a person; read "in evil," a condition. "This" in verse 20 follows both "the true one" and "Jesus Christ"; the Greek allows either, and the verse does not say which. John 17:3. "Eternal life," "know," "true God," "Jesus Christ": verse 20 has them all. Jeremiah 10:10. Against the idols of the verses before it, Yahweh is the true and living God. Verse 20 ends "the true God and eternal life"; verse 21, idols.
